js_003: Which ancient Greek epic poet is traditionally credited with writing The Iliad?
js_005: Hesiod, who sang of the gods’ genealogy
js_008: The Iliad is an epic traditionally credited to the ancient Greek poet Homer, around the 8th century BC. Along with The Odyssey, it’s considered one of the founding works of Western literature.
js_010: What’s the name of the decade-long war that serves as the backdrop for this epic?
js_012: The Peloponnesian War between Greek city-states
js_013: The Persian Wars, an invasion from the east
js_015: The setting is the Trojan War, a ten-year conflict between the Greek alliance and Troy. But the poem doesn’t cover the whole war — it zooms in on just a few weeks near the end.
js_017: Who stands at the center of The Iliad as the greatest warrior on the Greek side?
js_020: Agamemnon, commander of the allied forces
js_022: The protagonist is Achilles, son of a goddess and the greatest Greek warrior. His rage opens the story, and his reconciliation closes it.
js_024: What subject does the poet announce he will sing about in the opening lines of the epic?
js_025: The rage of Achilles and the disaster it caused
js_029: The very first word is the Greek ‘menis,’ meaning rage. The poet asks the goddess to sing of Achilles’s anger. The true subject of this epic isn’t war — it’s one man’s fury.
js_031: Who commands the Greek alliance that invades Troy?
js_036: The commander is Agamemnon, King of Mycenae. He’s the brother of Menelaus, whose wife was taken, and though he wields the greatest power, his clash with Achilles brings ruin on himself.
js_038: Who is the eldest prince and greatest warrior defending Troy?
js_040: Paris, who brought Helen to Troy
js_042: Aeneas, who later journeys to Rome
js_043: Troy’s pillar of strength is its eldest prince, Hector. Fighting to protect his wife and son, he’s portrayed as the most human hero in the entire epic.
js_045: Who is the Spartan queen that Paris brought to Troy, sparking the war?
js_049: Cassandra, the prophetess no one believed
js_050: The spark of the war is Sparta’s queen, Helen. When the Trojan prince Paris takes her to Troy, the Greek kings unite for a war of retribution.
js_052: Who is Achilles’s closest friend, killed while wearing Achilles’s own armor into battle?
js_057: Patroclus is Achilles’s inseparable friend. His death pulls Achilles back into the war and completely changes the direction of the story.
js_059: Where does the title ‘The Iliad’ come from?
js_063: A nickname for the war god Ares
js_064: Troy was also known as ‘Ilios’ (or Ilion). So the title of the epic essentially means ‘the song of Ilios.’
js_066: What’s the correct overall length and structure of The Iliad?
js_067: A long epic of twenty-four books and roughly 15,000 lines
js_068: A collection of short lyric poems
js_070: A two-act play meant only to be read aloud
js_071: The Iliad spans twenty-four books and about 15,693 lines, every line written in a fixed meter called dactylic hexameter.
js_084: Homer is traditionally dated to around the 8th century BC, though we can’t even be sure he actually existed. Both The Iliad and The Odyssey are attributed to his name.
js_085: The Trojan War is the legendary ten-year siege of Troy by the Greek alliance. The Iliad doesn’t cover the full decade — just a brief stretch near the very end.
js_086: Achilles is the son of the goddess Thetis and the mortal Peleus. Destined to die young, he chooses glory over a long life, making him the central figure of the epic.
js_087: The poem’s first word is the Greek ‘menis,’ meaning rage. Right from line one, the poet declares that the true subject isn’t the whole war, but one man’s anger.
js_088: Agamemnon is King of Mycenae and commander of the allied forces. He holds the most power, but his poor judgment repeatedly puts him at odds with his greatest warrior, at great cost.
js_089: Hector is King Priam’s eldest son and Troy’s shield. He fights not for glory but to protect his family and city, standing in sharp contrast to Achilles.
js_090: Helen was the wife of King Menelaus of Sparta. When Paris takes her to Troy, the Greek kings, bound by oath, unite their forces and set sail.
js_091: Patroclus is Achilles’s closest friend. His death is the turning point that shifts Achilles’s rage away from Agamemnon and onto Hector.
js_092: Troy was also called ‘Ilios’ (or Ilion). ‘Iliad’ comes from that name, meaning ‘a song about Ilios.’
js_093: The Iliad has twenty-four books and about 15,693 lines. The book divisions are believed to have been organized later by scholars in Alexandria.
js_106: ↻ This question will come back later
js_108: The epic’s first word and central theme. Not the war as a whole, but the rage of one man, Achilles, drives the entire story.
js_110: Fame passed down in song, outliving death itself. For a mortal bound to die, it was the one path to touching eternity.
js_112: A visible token of honor, like a war prize. It’s why losing Briseis wasn’t about property — it was a blow to Achilles’s very worth.
js_114: Hephaestus forges a shield engraved with weddings, trials, harvests, and dances — an entire life pictured in the middle of a war.
js_116: Hera, Athena, and Poseidon back the Greeks; Apollo, Aphrodite, and Ares back the Trojans. The gods’ own quarrels sway the battle below.
js_118: A hero who fights not for glory but to protect his family and city. Their farewell scene in Book 6 is the most human moment in the epic.
js_120: An old king kisses the hands of the man who killed his son. The epic, opened by rage, closes in Book 24 with an act of mercy.
js_122: Repeated phrases like ‘swift-footed Achilles’ helped bards improvise on the spot — a trace of oral formulas identified by scholar Milman Parry.
js_125: Apollo sends a plague that ravages the Greek camp.
js_126: Agamemnon seizes Briseis, Achilles’s war prize.
js_127: Humiliated, Achilles lays down his weapons and withdraws.
js_128: His mother Thetis asks Zeus to let the Greeks lose without him.
js_129: A truce and a duel fall apart, and full war breaks out again.
js_131: A Day of Heroes — Gods and Mortals Collide
js_132: Diomedes goes on a rampage, even wounding gods in battle.
js_133: Hector returns to the city to say goodbye to Andromache and their son.
js_134: He takes off his helmet so his crying son won’t be scared of it.
js_135: Hector and Ajax duel, then part as friends, trading gifts.
js_136: Zeus steps in, and the tide begins to turn toward Troy.
js_138: Refusal and Retreat — Ships Set Ablaze
js_139: Agamemnon sends envoys bearing a mountain of gifts.
js_140: Achilles refuses — no gift can undo a broken honor.
js_141: One by one, the Greeks’ best fighters fall wounded and retreat.
js_142: The Trojans breach the wall and try to torch the ships.
js_143: The whole army pays the price for Achilles’s absence.
js_146: Patroclus borrows Achilles’s armor and joins the fight.
js_147: He pushes the enemy back but forgets the warning and charges the walls.
js_148: With Apollo’s help, Hector strikes him down.
js_149: Hearing the news, Achilles howls in grief in the dust.
js_150: Hephaestus forges him a new shield overnight.
js_153: Achilles makes peace with Agamemnon and returns to battle.
js_154: His rage rages so fierce he even fights a river god.
js_155: Hector is chased three times around the city walls before turning to face him.
js_157: He drags the body behind his chariot in a final act of disgrace.
js_159: Funeral Games and a Night of Peace
js_160: Patroclus is given a funeral, followed by memorial games.
js_161: Priam slips alone into the enemy camp in the dead of night.
js_162: He kisses the hand of his son’s killer and begs for the body.
js_163: Achilles thinks of his own father, and the two men weep together.
js_164: The body is returned, and the epic ends with Hector’s funeral.
js_165: The Father Who Removed His Helmet
js_166: When Hector comes to say goodbye and his son bursts into tears at the sight of his gleaming helmet, he takes it off, sets it down, and lifts the child into his arms.
js_167: A warrior’s pride and a father’s tenderness meet in a single moment. What ‘helmet’ do you put on and take off every day?
js_169: Agamemnon offers gold, horses, even cities to make peace — and Achilles turns it all down.
js_170: A declaration that some wounds can’t be repaired with compensation. How far can an apology actually undo the damage?
js_171: Kissing the Hand of an Enemy
js_172: Priam walks alone into the tent of the man who killed his son, kisses his hand, and begs for the body. The two sit and weep together.
js_173: What ends the cycle of revenge isn’t victory — it’s compassion. Is it strength that stops hatred, or shared grief?
js_174: A short, blazing life or a long, ordinary one — which would you choose?
js_175: Knowing both fates, Achilles chose the first. Ask yourself what matters more: what you want to leave behind, or what you want to hold onto.
js_176: When something upsets me most, is it the loss itself — or the feeling of being disrespected?
js_177: What drove Achilles to walk away wasn’t the loss of property — it was his honor. Think back to a recent argument: what actually stung?
js_178: In stories of glory, whose name gets mentioned but whose voice never does?
js_179: Briseis and Chryseis are central to the plot, yet they barely speak. Think about whose voice is missing from the stories you read.
